strengths: The paper targets a real limitation of reservoir computing—sequential processing and quadratic memory in reservoir size—and proposes a simple, well-motivated architecture that replaces dense recurrent connections with diagonal complex linear recurrence, enabling associative-scan parallelization and large memory savings.

The theoretical ESP analysis (Theorem 4.1) for diagonal linear reservoirs is correct and practically useful: it gives a simple necessary and sufficient condition |lambda_i|<1 and connects it to the initialization of eigenvalues, leakage, and spectral radius.

The empirical study is broad and carefully reported: it covers memory-based tasks, chaotic forecasting, real-world forecasting, UEA/UCR classification, and sMNIST/psMNIST, with efficiency metrics (training time, energy, CO2) and statistical ranking.
The reported speed/memory advantages are substantial, and the model often reaches accuracy competitive with or better than traditional ESNs, especially in deep configurations.
Appendix provides useful details on datasets, hyperparameter ranges, model selection, and computational resources, which aids reproducibility.
The method is easy to implement on top of existing parallel-scan/SSM tooling, making it practically useful for RC practitioners.
weaknesses: The central universality claim is not rigorously established for the proposed architecture. Proposition 4.2 assumes every linear transition matrix is exactly diagonalizable; defective matrices are not, and 'up to arbitrarily small perturbations' does not prove exact equivalence. Moreover, the proof treats f_out as an arbitrary MLP on the reservoir state, while the actual ParalESN has a fixed random mixing layer f_mix before the trainable readout. There is no proof that f_readout composed with f_mix can realize the required MLP, so Corollary 4.3 does not directly apply to the model as defined.

The complexity analysis overstates parallel speedup. Associative scan has O(T) work and O(log T) depth; Table 5's O(log(T) N_h N_in) whole-sequence time is only valid under unbounded parallelism, not for standard wall-clock complexity. The empirical log scaling may not hold generally.

Novelty is incremental: diagonal complex linear recurrence and parallel scan are well known from LRU/SSMs; applying them to an untrained reservoir with a random local mixer and ridge/MLP readout is a straightforward combination rather than a fundamentally new RC paradigm.

Baseline comparisons with fully trainable models are not fully convincing. For example, Mamba reaches only 92.6% on psMNIST, below typical reported results, suggesting under-tuning; architecture choices for LSTM/Transformer/LRU/Mamba are fixed and only learning rate/weight decay are searched. This weakens the claim of competitiveness.

Efficiency claims are overbroad: on sMNIST, ParalESN vs. LRU is roughly 10x faster and ~14x lower energy, not 'orders of magnitude'; the phrase is only accurate for some baselines (e.g., Transformer).

The paper lacks an explicit limitations section and does not release code or seeds. Hyperparameter search details (number of Bayesian trials, exact search budgets per model) are incomplete, limiting reproducibility.

Several notation and presentation issues remain (e.g., h_t^(ell) dimension written as N_in, Lambda_n typo, inconsistent use of hat-Lambda_h and Lambda_h), and the role of the local 1-D convolution in theoretical expressivity is not ablated.

strengths: Addresses a real bottleneck in Reservoir Computing: sequential processing and the memory footprint of dense high-dimensional reservoirs.
Proposes a parallelizable design using diagonal complex linear recurrence and associative scan, which is practically efficient on modern hardware.
Provides some theoretical grounding, including a sufficient and necessary condition for the Echo State Property in the linear diagonal case.

Conducts an extensive empirical evaluation across memory-based tasks, forecasting, time-series classification, and pixel-level classification, comparing against traditional RC and fully trainable models (LSTM, Transformer, LRU, Mamba).
Reports substantial computational savings in training time, energy consumption, and CO2 emissions on several benchmarks, especially sMNIST and psMNIST.
The deep variant with mixing layers yields strong classification accuracy and remains efficient.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core mechanism (diagonal complex linear recurrence with associative scan) is directly adopted from LRU/SSMs; applying it to RC with an untrained reservoir and a random convolution mixer is incremental and not sufficiently differentiated from existing SSM/LRU approaches.

Theoretical analysis has flaws: Proposition 4.2 states that 'every square matrix is diagonalizable in the complex field, up to arbitrarily small perturbations,' which is false as stated; exact equivalence to arbitrary linear reservoirs is not established. The universality corollary assumes an arbitrary MLP readout, but most experiments use ridge regression (linear readout), so the practical model is not covered by the universality claim.

Complexity analysis contains an error and an overclaim: Table 5 lists ESN whole-sequence time as O(T N_h^3), contradicting the text (O(T N_h^2)). More importantly, ParalESN's whole-sequence complexity is listed as O(log(T) N_h N_in), conflating parallel depth with total work; the total work of associative scan is O(T N_h N_in), so the claimed logarithmic time complexity is misleading.

Empirical claims are overstated: the abstract says ParalESN 'matches the predictive accuracy of traditional RC,' but Tables 1 and 2 show it is worse on several tasks (e.g., ctXOR5, ctXOR10, SinMem20, NARMA10). On sMNIST, its accuracy is 1–2% below fully trainable models, which may not qualify as 'competitive.'

Efficiency comparison omits the cost of hyperparameter search: model selection uses up to 24 hours of Bayesian search per model, which could substantially reduce the claimed efficiency advantage. The paper does not report total search time or the best hyperparameters found.
Reproducibility is limited: no code or data generation scripts are provided, and the exact best configurations are not reported, making it difficult for others to reproduce the results.

No limitations section: the paper does not discuss potential drawbacks such as sensitivity to hyperparameters, the fixed random mixing function, the use of complex arithmetic, or the gap to fully trainable models. Only an appendix sensitivity analysis is included.
Presentation issues: typos in equations (e.g., \Lambda_{\text{n}} in Eq. 4), a confusing Figure 1 caption, and the erroneous complexity table reduce clarity.

strengths: Addresses a real bottleneck in reservoir computing by replacing dense sequential recurrence with diagonal complex linear recurrence, enabling parallel processing via associative scan; Figure 2 demonstrates logarithmic recurrence time and scaling to high-dimensional reservoirs where traditional ESNs run out of memory.

Provides a clean theoretical condition for the Echo State Property in diagonal linear reservoirs (Theorem 4.1: ESP iff all effective diagonal eigenvalues have modulus < 1) and an equivalence result showing that arbitrary linear reservoirs can be represented in complex diagonal form (Proposition 4.2).

Extensive empirical evaluation spans memory-based tasks (MemCap, ctXOR, SinMem), forecasting (Lorenz96, Mackey-Glass, NARMA, ETT), time-series classification (UEA/UCR), and 1-D pixel-level tasks (sMNIST/psMNIST), with strong baselines including ESNs, deep ESNs, LSTM, Transformer, LRU, and Mamba.

Demonstrates substantial efficiency gains: order-of-magnitude faster training and lower energy/CO2 emissions, e.g., on sMNIST ParalESN trains in 2.7 min versus 29.1 min for LRU and 141 min for Transformer, with energy 0.04 KWh versus 0.57/1.81 KWh.

Achieves competitive accuracy in several settings, e.g., sMNIST 97.2% versus 82.5% for ESN and 91.4% for deep ESN; psMNIST 96.9% versus 78.2% for ESN; and improvements over shallow ESNs on multiple UEA/UCR classification tasks.
Appendix provides detailed reproducibility information: dataset descriptions, hyperparameter search ranges, model-selection protocol, computational resources, and energy tracking via CodeCarbon.
The work is practically significant for scaling reservoir computing to larger reservoirs and longer sequences while retaining the RC paradigm of training only a lightweight readout.
weaknesses: The universality claim is not fully supported for the actual architecture. Corollary 4.3 relies on an MLP readout and absorbs the fixed mixing function into an arbitrary trainable f_out, but many experiments (memory-based, forecasting, UEA/UCR classification) use a linear ridge readout, so the theoretical universality guarantee does not directly apply. The practical model with fixed random convolution+tanh mixing followed by a linear readout is not proven universal.

Proposition 4.2 uses diagonalizability of arbitrary matrices 'up to arbitrarily small perturbations,' but many matrices are defective; exact equivalence, conditioning of the diagonalizing transform, and approximation error are not discussed. This weakens the claimed equivalence to arbitrary linear reservoirs.

The novelty is incremental: the core mechanism is essentially an LRU-style diagonal linear recurrence combined with a fixed random convolution+tanh mixing layer and a trained readout. The theoretical results are straightforward consequences of known linear-system stability and diagonalization.

There is no explicit limitations section. The paper does not discuss cases where ParalESN underperforms, e.g., psMNIST deep 95.2% versus shallow 96.9%, NARMA10 3.7 versus 2.7 for ESN, and MG84 5.2 versus 4.2 for deep ESN.

Parameter comparisons are ambiguous. Table 4 labels 'PARAMS.' without clarifying whether these are trainable or total parameters; for RC models this likely counts only trainable readout parameters, while for fully trainable models it counts all parameters. Also, the MLP readout used for MNIST adds trainable hidden layers, so the 'only readout is trainable' framing is nuanced.
The theoretical ESP analysis is limited to one-layer ParalESN; deep configurations are not analyzed, even though deep models are a major part of the experiments.

Presentation contains errors and inconsistencies: Table 5 lists ESN whole-sequence complexity as O(T N_h^3) while the text states O(T N_h^2); Table 4 reports energy 0.04±0.1 KWh, which is implausible; and Figure 3's caption has grammatical issues.
No code or reproducibility artifact is mentioned, which limits reliable adoption despite the detailed hyperparameter descriptions.
